artworks.title: Orpheus
artworks.description: A Thracian girl cradles Orpheus' severed head where it has come to rest on his own lyre, head and instrument fused into a single relic. Moreau turns the myth's most violent moment into still, jewelled mourning; the painting entered the French state collections in his lifetime and now hangs in the Musée d'Orsay, Paris.

artworks.title: Orpheus Leading Eurydice from the Underworld
artworks.description: Corot's silvery twilight catches the pair mid-passage: Orpheus lifts his lyre like a lantern while Eurydice follows a half-step behind, the fatal backward glance only moments away. Museum of Fine Arts, Houston.

films.title: Orphée
films.description: Cocteau moves the poet to postwar Paris, where Death rides in a Rolls-Royce, messages come over car radio, and mirrors are the doors to the underworld — the central panel of his Orphic film trilogy.

films.title: Black Orpheus
films.description: The myth replayed across Rio de Janeiro's Carnival to the bossa nova of Jobim and Bonfá: a tram-driver Orpheus, a country-girl Eurydice, and Death in a skeleton suit. It took both the Palme d'Or and the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.

music.title: L'Orfeo
music.description: Monteverdi's favola in musica for the Mantuan court is the earliest opera still in regular repertory — the newborn art form chose the singer who could move the underworld as its founding subject.

music.title: Orfeo ed Euridice
music.description: Gluck's Viennese 'reform opera' strips the myth to its grief and lets the drama drive the music; the lament 'Che farò senza Euridice?' became one of opera's most famous arias.

music.title: Hadestown
music.description: Mitchell's folk-and-jazz retelling grew from a concept album into a Broadway musical, setting Orpheus' vow against Hades' industrial underworld; it won eight Tony Awards including Best Musical.
